title: Asset Sale or Share Sale: The Structure Question That Changes What You Actually Walk Away With
excerpt: Two businesses can sell for the same headline price and leave their owners with very different outcomes, because of a structure decision buyers usually raise first, not sellers.
content:
Two businesses can sell for the exact same headline price and leave their owners with genuinely different outcomes. Not because either side negotiated badly, but because somewhere in the process a decision got made about how the sale would actually happen, and that decision reshapes what is being sold far more than most sellers expect going in.

That decision is whether the sale is structured as an asset sale or a share sale. It usually gets raised by the buyer's lawyer a few weeks into the process, framed as a technical point for the lawyers to sort out. For the seller, it is rarely technical. It changes what is being transferred, who keeps responsibility for what came before, and how cleanly the deal actually closes.

Most owners spend years thinking about price and almost no time thinking about structure, simply because nobody has ever walked them through what the choice actually involves before a buyer is sitting across the table with a preference of their own.

Two Different Things Called Selling the Business

A share sale transfers the company itself, the legal entity, with everything that sits inside it. The buyer inherits the existing contracts, leases, licences and employment arrangements largely intact, because nothing has changed hands except who owns the shares. It also means the buyer inherits the company's history, its past tax positions, any dispute sitting quietly in the background, and any liability that hasn't surfaced yet.

An asset sale is a different transaction entirely. The buyer purchases specific assets, stock, equipment and goodwill, sometimes the trading name, out of the existing entity rather than the entity itself. The old company, and whatever history sits inside it, stays with the seller. Contracts, leases and licences don't automatically come along for the ride. Each one has to be individually assigned or novated to the buyer, and whoever sits on the other side of that contract, a landlord, a key supplier, a regulator, has to agree to the change.

Why the Preference Usually Isn't the Seller's

Buyers lean toward asset sales more often than sellers do, and the pattern across most transactions comes down to the same reason: an asset sale lets a buyer choose exactly what they're taking on and leave the rest behind. They aren't exposed to a tax position they didn't create, a dispute they didn't cause, or an old liability that surfaces eighteen months after settlement. From where the buyer is sitting, that's simply good risk management.

From the seller's side, the same structure creates work the headline price never mentions. Every material contract and lease needs a counterparty's sign off to move across, and there is no guarantee every one of them says yes on the same terms. Employee entitlements need to be handled carefully through the transfer. None of this shows up in the number on the term sheet, but it shows up in how smoothly the deal actually closes, and sometimes in how much gets held back or renegotiated once the buyer's due diligence starts working through the detail.

In practice, this tension often turns up as a line inside the negotiation rather than a separate conversation. A buyer might propose a lower price for a share sale to compensate for the risk they are inheriting, or ask for a longer settlement period in an asset sale so every contract can be reassigned before completion. Structure and price are rarely decided independently of each other, even when they get discussed as if they were.

What to Settle Before the Buyer Frames It for You

The tax treatment of each structure is genuinely different, and it is exactly the kind of question that belongs with your accountant rather than in a blog post, since it depends on entity structure, history and individual circumstances in ways a general article never can responsibly cover. What a business owner can get ahead of is everything else: which key contracts and leases would need a counterparty's consent, how clean the entity's history actually is, and whether the business is more saleable as a share sale or an asset sale given its own structure.

This is precisely the kind of question an Exit Readiness Diagnostic is built to surface well before a buyer is in the room, scoring the contracts, the entity and the other buyer-grade dimensions so the structure conversation starts from a position of knowledge rather than reacting to whatever the other side proposes first. Pairing that with an indicative read on value early gives an owner a baseline for both price and structure before either one is being negotiated under pressure.

The number on the term sheet is the headline. The structure underneath it is what actually determines what lands in the seller's account, when, and with how much risk still attached. Most owners only learn the difference the first time someone else raises it. The ones who raise it first tend to like the outcome more.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an asset sale and a share sale in Australia?
faqs.a: In a share sale, the buyer takes over the entire legal entity, including its history, past tax positions and any dispute that hasn't surfaced yet. In an asset sale, the buyer purchases specific assets, stock and goodwill out of the business, while the existing entity and its history stay with the seller. Contracts, leases and licences each need individual consent to transfer across.

faqs.q: Why do buyers often prefer an asset sale over a share sale?
faqs.a: An asset sale lets a buyer choose exactly which assets, contracts and liabilities they take on, and leave the rest with the seller's existing entity. That avoids inheriting a tax position, a dispute or a liability they had no part in creating. It's a reasonable way for a buyer to manage risk, even though it usually creates more transfer work for the seller. Our exit readiness guide covers this in more detail.

faqs.q: Does an asset sale or a share sale change how much tax I pay on sale?
faqs.a: The tax treatment of each structure can differ meaningfully, and it depends on entity structure, history and individual circumstances in ways no general answer can cover responsibly. This is a conversation to have directly with your accountant once a sale is realistically on the table, alongside the commercial and structural side of the decision.

faqs.q: What happens to employee entitlements when a business is sold through an asset sale?
faqs.a: Employee arrangements need careful, deliberate handling in an asset sale, since employment doesn't automatically continue the way it does in a share sale. Entitlements, continuity of service and transfer terms all need to be worked through as part of the deal, which is one of the practical reasons asset sales often take longer to close than the headline price suggests.

faqs.q: Can a landlord or supplier block an asset sale by refusing to transfer a contract?
faqs.a: Yes. Contracts, leases and licences generally need the other party's consent to move across to a new buyer in an asset sale, and there's no guarantee they agree on the same terms. A landlord or key supplier who says no, or asks for new terms, can genuinely slow a deal down or change its economics partway through.

faqs.q: When should a business owner decide between an asset sale and a share sale?
faqs.a: Well before a buyer is in the room, ideally as part of broader exit preparation rather than as a reaction to the buyer's first proposal. Understanding which structure actually fits the business, alongside an indicative read on value, gives an owner a baseline to negotiate from instead of accepting whichever structure the other side suggests first.
